J Clin Oncol 2003; 21: 4642–9. ACUTE LYMPHOBLASTIC LEUKAEMIA. With current chemotherapy regimens, long-term disease free surviv- al can be achieved in over 80% of children and 30 to 40% of adults with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL).1 While there is a lack of consensus on some prognostic factors, it is generally accepted that age less than 1 year or greater than 10 years, and high white cell count at the time of diagnosis indicate patients at higher risk of relapse.2 These factors probably reflect the pres- ence of specific genotypes. Chromosomal transloca- tions that activate specific genes are a defining charac- teristic of ALL; although genetic abnormalities do not entirely account for treatment outcome they do provide prognostic information. In general, patients with chang- es such as hyperdiploidy, TEL-AML1 fusion, or t(1;19)/E2A-PBX1 fusion have the most favourable outcome, whereas those with t(9;22)/BCR-ABL fusion (the Philadelphia chromosome) or t(4;11)/MLL-AF4 fusion have a poorer outcome. More than 50% of cases of T-cell ALL have activating mutations that involve NOTCH1, a gene encoding a receptor that regulates normal T-cell development.2 Standard treatment regimens for T-cell and precursor B- cell ALL generally consist of 2 to 3 years of therapy divid- ed into several phases: a short remission-induction phase; an intensification (consolidation) phase; therapy for prophylaxis of CNS disease, starting during the induction phase, and sometimes continuing for an extended period; and a prolonged continuation (maintenance) phase, some- times including re-induction therapy.1-3 Treatment for ma- ture B-cell ALL (Burkitt cell leukaemia or lymphoma, see Burkitt’s Lymphoma, below) is different in terms of the drugs used, and the maintenance phase is not required.1,2 The aim of induction therapy is to induce complete re- mission, and a slow early response to this therapy has been reported to be an indicator of poor prognosis.4 Measure- ment of minimal residual disease at completion of induc- tion therapy is particularly useful in determining progno- sis.3 Standard induction regimens include vincristine and a cor- ticosteroid (prednisolone or prednisone, or dexametha- sone), plus asparaginase in children and an anthracycline such as doxorubicin in adults.
